"Shelf Swap" wins for a neighbor-to-neighbor book trading app:

- **It says what it does.** "Swap" names the core action, and "shelf" instantly signals books. A new user grasps the concept before reading a single line of description.
- **Alliteration makes it stick.** Two stressed syllables, easy to say aloud — which matters for an app that spreads by word of mouth among neighbors.
- **It scales into a verb and a vocabulary.** "Let's set up a swap," "swap history," "swap radius." Product language writes itself.

"Dog-Ear" is the more charming name, and I'd keep it in a back pocket for a feature (a "dog-ear" as a save/bookmark action would be lovely). But as the app name it has real drawbacks: it evokes a solitary reading habit rather than an exchange between people, dog-earing connotes damaging a book — odd for a service built on passing books along in decent shape — and a fair number of users will first think it's about dogs.

The one case where A would beat B: if you're deliberately building a cozy, personality-forward brand in a crowded market where clarity is table stakes and distinctiveness is the scarce thing. But for a local, trust-dependent service that lives or dies on people understanding it fast, clarity wins.

A lunging, roaring mount does something a placid walking pose can't: it grabs you by the collar. Museums compete with screens for attention, and a 40-foot theropod caught mid-strike is what makes a seven-year-old stop, look up, and decide that paleontology is the most interesting thing in the world. That moment of awe is the actual product a science museum sells.

The usual objection is that dramatic poses are sensationalized and that animals mostly just walk around. True, but "mostly just walking around" is a fact about *averages*, not a reason to display the average. A skeleton in motion also teaches better anatomy — you can see how the tail counterbalanced the body, how the limbs loaded under stress, how the whole animal worked as a machine. A neutral standing pose tends to read as furniture.

That said, the roar should be defensible: no tripod-tail dragging, no upright kangaroo stance, jaws opened only as far as the joint allows. Drama and accuracy aren't actually in tension — the Field Museum's SUE and the AMNH *Barosaurus* rearing over its calf are both thrilling *and* biomechanically argued. That's the target.

Letting teams work puzzles in any order is generally the stronger format for a community contest. It prevents a single hard puzzle from stalling everyone, lets teams play to their varied strengths (wordplay, logic, trivia, physical construction), keeps parallel work possible so larger teams stay engaged, and reduces the need for you to calibrate difficulty into a perfect ascending ladder. It also makes hint-giving less time-critical, since a stuck team has other things to do while waiting.

Sequential release does have real virtues — a shared narrative arc, everyone experiencing the same moment together, easier live commentary and leaderboard drama — so it can be the better pick if your event is short, spectator-facing, or story-driven. But for most community puzzle hunts, open order plus a final meta-puzzle that requires several answers gives you both freedom and a satisfying climax.

Clay is the better choice for a short stop-motion piece about an imaginary town. It's a genuinely three-dimensional medium, so you can build streets, rooftops, and characters that hold their own shape under lights and read convincingly from multiple camera angles. More importantly, clay holds an incremental pose — you can nudge a figure's arm or lean a chimney a few millimeters between frames and it stays put, which is exactly what frame-by-frame animation demands. It's also forgiving: if a pose doesn't work, you reshape it rather than recutting and rebuilding.

Paper cutouts are a legitimate and lovely technique, but they lock you into flat, largely overhead or straight-on shooting, and pieces tend to shift or curl as you handle them. For invented architecture especially, you lose the depth and physical texture that sell a town as a real place.

**A**

Clay gives you true three-dimensional sets and characters, so you can light them, shoot from varied angles, and get real depth — useful for conveying a whole town. It also holds its position between frames and can be incrementally reshaped, which is exactly what stop-motion requires (squash a roof, bend an arm, nudge a figure a few millimeters). Paper cutouts are flat, tend to shift or curl, and generally lock you into a fixed overhead camera setup.

Letting the puppets build their own world in front of the audience is the stronger opening. It does several things at once:

- **It establishes the puppets as agents**, not props. Before they've spoken a line, they've demonstrated will, effort, and purpose — the audience grants them life on their own terms rather than being asked to accept it.
- **It teaches the visual grammar of the show.** The audience learns what a wall means, what a door means, how scale works — so later transformations read instantly instead of needing explanation.
- **It invites complicity rather than passivity.** A revealed set says "believe this." A built set says "help me believe this," which is a far more durable kind of engagement, especially with puppetry, where the audience is already doing the imaginative work of ignoring rods and hands.
- **It creates suspense from nothing.** Watching something become is inherently more interesting than seeing something that already is.

Option A's real advantage is the gasp — a lush, detailed reveal can land hard, and if your show depends on spectacle or a single overwhelming image, that's worth something. It's also simply faster, which matters for short pieces or young audiences with little patience.

But the reveal spends its capital immediately and has nowhere to go. The assembly opening earns the same delight while also arming the audience for everything that follows.

**A**

Having the puppets build their own world in full view is the stronger opening. It immediately establishes them as agents rather than objects — the audience watches inanimate figures take on intention, which is the core pleasure of puppetry. It also invites the audience into complicity with the illusion: they see the strings, the seams, the hands, and choose to believe anyway. That shared agreement is more binding than a concealed trick.

A revealed curtain, by contrast, hides the labor and asks the audience to accept a finished world. It can be beautiful, but it spends its surprise in one moment and teaches the audience to expect polish rather than play. The assembly opening earns attention gradually and sets up a language of visible mechanics that the rest of the show can exploit — a rock lifted and carried, a sun hoisted on a pole, a puppet handing another its own prop.

The one case for B is a show built on atmosphere or a sudden tonal shock, where the reveal itself is the dramatic event. But for most puppet shows, especially ones with comedy or a young audience, A does more work.

Letting the puppets build their own world in front of the audience is the stronger opening. It does several things at once:

- **It establishes the puppets as agents** before they've said a word. They aren't decorations placed inside a set; they're the ones who make the set exist. That reframes everything that follows.
- **It invites complicity rather than concealment.** Puppetry's power comes from an audience that knowingly participates in the illusion. Hiding the mechanics behind a curtain fights that instinct; revealing them harnesses it. Audiences delight in seeing the seams and choosing to believe anyway.
- **It gives you a built-in first act of physical comedy or wonder** — a table too heavy, a backdrop hung crooked, a tiny puppet dragging an enormous prop. Pure visual storytelling, no exposition required.
- **It teaches the audience the rules.** They learn the scale, the logic, and the tone of this world by watching it get assembled.

A revealed set is a single beat: a gasp, then it's spent. An assembled set is a sequence that accumulates meaning.

The case for A isn't nothing, though. If your show depends on a genuine spectacle — an elaborate, gasp-worthy tableau — or on a sense of mystery and dread where mechanics would puncture the mood, the curtain reveal earns its keep. Certain traditions (formal marionette theatre, some shadow puppetry) also rely on an unbroken illusion.

But as a default, and especially for anything playful or handmade in spirit, B is the richer choice.

The lead actor stuck on last year's lines is the stronger engine, for a few reasons:

**It's a character problem, not a logistics problem.** Comedy escalates best when the trouble lives inside someone who has something to lose — pride, a crush in the audience, a last shot at the lead role. The prop mix-up happens *to* the cast; the line problem happens *in* someone, so every scene can carry emotional stakes alongside the jokes.

**It generates inexhaustible, specific gags.** Every wrong line is a collision between two texts, and you get to choose which two. *Our Town* bleeding into *Macbeth* writes its own punchlines, and the audience gets the pleasure of recognizing the seam. Wrong props give you one joke shape — "that's not the right object" — repeated with different nouns.

**It forces everyone else to act.** Other characters must improvise around him, cover for him, sabotage or rescue him. That creates alliances, betrayals, and a whole subplot economy. Misdelivered props mostly produce shrugging and scrambling.

**It builds to a real climax.** You can land the ending on whether he finally says the right line — or whether the "wrong" line turns out to be exactly what the moment needed. Props can't carry a thematic payoff that cleanly.

That said, B makes an excellent *secondary* runner — a low-grade absurdity humming in the background while the real pressure comes from the actor. If you want both, let the props be the B-story that occasionally makes his problem worse.

**A**

The lead actor stuck on last year's lines is the stronger engine, for a few reasons:

**It's character-based, not logistics-based.** A misfiring actor has an interior problem — panic, ego, denial — that other characters must react to, negotiate with, and work around. Wrong props are an external inconvenience; someone just has to solve a delivery problem.

**It generates conflict between people.** Every wrong line forces the other actors to improvise, cover, or sabotage him, which puts the whole cast in the joke. Misdelivered props mostly put the stage manager in the joke.

**It escalates onstage, in front of an audience.** The comedy detonates at the worst possible moment with witnesses, which is where farce wants to live. Props tend to create backstage scrambling — funny, but a preparation problem you can technically fix before curtain.

**It has a built-in payoff.** Last year's play is a specific, knowable text, so you can seed the collision early and let the two scripts fight each other for the whole third act. You can also use it emotionally: the actor clinging to last year's triumph is quietly poignant, which gives the farce a floor.

**Practical note:** B isn't useless — it's a great *secondary* runner. A Roman spear showing up for a Tennessee Williams production is a solid recurring gag that supports A without competing with it. Complications that stack tend to beat complications that duplicate, and these two work at different levels: one human, one material.

**B**

The lead actor reciting last year's lines is the stronger comic engine, for a few reasons:

- **It's active, not incidental.** A wrong prop sits there being funny once; a wrong actor keeps generating problems in real time. Every scene partner has to improvise around him, so the complication spreads outward and escalates.
- **It creates character.** Someone confidently wrong is inherently funnier than an inanimate object being wrong.
